title: Amplitude Modulation (AM): Generation, Envelope Analysis & Power Efficiency

content.aim: To generate amplitude-modulated signals using TPS-3421 trainer, measure modulation index from envelope parameters, observe under-modulation, critical modulation and over-modulation, and analyze time-domain envelope and frequency-domain sidebands, including power distribution and efficiency.
objectives: To understand need for modulation for wireless transmission regarding antenna size and frequency division multiplexing.
To generate double-sideband full-carrier (DSB-FC) AM waves using four-quadrant multiplier.
To measure Vmax and Vmin of modulated envelope on oscilloscope and calculate modulation index m = (Vmax-Vmin)/(Vmax+Vmin).
To investigate under-modulation (m<1), critical modulation (m=1) and over-modulation (m>1) with envelope distortion and phase reversal.
To identify carrier at fc, lower sideband at fc-fm and upper sideband at fc+fm and confirm bandwidth BW=2fm.
To measure power distribution between carrier and sidebands and evaluate efficiency η = m²/(2+m²)*100%.
To examine effect of non-sinusoidal modulating waveform (triangle) on envelope symmetry and harmonic sidebands.

theory.text:
Need for Modulation

Baseband audio signals (20Hz-20kHz) cannot be directly radiated efficiently:

• Antenna size: Efficient radiation requires antenna length L ≥ λ/4. For 1kHz audio, λ = c/f = 3×10⁸/1×10³ = 300km, so L ≥75km, impracticable. Modulating onto 800kHz carrier gives λ=375m, L≈94m, feasible.

• Channel multiplexing: Without modulation, all stations would share same low-frequency spectrum causing interference. Modulation shifts each signal to distinct carrier frequency (FDM).

Mathematical Description of AM

Let modulating signal be:

\[\mathit{v}_{m}(t) = \mathit{V}_{m} \cos(\omega _{m} t)\]

Carrier:

\[\mathit{v}_{c}(t) = \mathit{V}_{c} \cos(\omega _{c} t)\] with fc >> fm.

In AM, carrier amplitude varies proportionally to modulating signal:

\[\mathit{V}_{AM}(t) = \mathit{V}_{c} + \mathit{V}_{m} \cos(\omega _{m} t)\]

Modulated wave:

\[\mathit{v}_{AM}(t) = [\mathit{V}_{c} + \mathit{V}_{m} \cos(\omega _{m} t)] \cos(\omega _{c} t) = \mathit{V}_{c}[1+m\cos(\omega _{m} t)]\cos(\omega _{c} t)\]

where modulation index m = Vm/Vc

Envelope and Modulation Index

On oscilloscope, envelope peaks give Vmax and Vmin (peak-to-peak):

Vmax = 2(Vc+Vm)
Vmin = 2(Vc-Vm)

Vc = (Vmax+Vmin)/4
Vm = (Vmax-Vmin)/4
m = (Vmax-Vmin)/(Vmax+Vmin)

Three regimes:

• Under-modulation (0<m<1): Vmin>0, envelope never reaches zero, envelope mirrors audio without clipping. Standard broadcast condition. At m=0.5, Vmax=6V, Vmin=2V, clean envelope observed.

• Critical (m=1): Vm=Vc, Vmin=0, envelope touches zero axis. Maximum sideband power without distortion. At m=1, Vmax=8V, Vmin=0V measured.

• Over-modulation (m>1): Vm>Vc, multiplier attempts to drive carrier negative, causing 180° phase reversal when 1+mcos(ωmt)<0. Envelope pinches and inverts. Envelope detector cannot track phase reversal, leading to clipping, distortion and adjacent-channel splatter. Observed at m=1.25 with crossover and phase inversion.

Spectral Analysis and Bandwidth

Using cosA cosB = ½[cos(A-B)+cos(A+B)]:

\[\mathit{v}_{AM}(t) = \mathit{V}_{c}\cos(\omega _{c} t) + \frac{m\mathit{V}_{c}}{2}\cos[(\omega _{c}-\omega _{m})t] + \frac{m\mathit{V}_{c}}{2}\cos[(\omega _{c}+\omega _{m})t]\]

Components: Carrier at fc amplitude Vc (no information), LSB at fc-fm amplitude mVc/2, USB at fc+fm amplitude mVc/2.

Bandwidth:

BW = fUSB - fLSB = (fc+fm)-(fc-fm) = 2fm

Bandwidth depends only on modulating frequency, not carrier. For voice limited to 5kHz, AM channel is 10kHz.

Power Distribution and Efficiency

For load R:

• Carrier power Pc = Vc²/(2R)

• Each sideband PLSB = PUSB = (mVc/2)²/(2R) = m²/4 Pc

• Total sideband PSB = m²/2 Pc

• Total transmitted Pt = Pc(1+m²/2)

Efficiency (useful sideband power / total):

η = PSB/Pt = m²/(2+m²) *100%

At m=1, ηmax = 1/3 =33.33%. Two-thirds of power wasted in carrier, each sideband carries 16.67%. Average speech/music with m≈0.3-0.4 gives efficiency <8%, motivating SSB-SC and FM.

Comparison with Other Schemes

DSB-FC is inefficient because carrier contains no information and two sidebands carry identical information (redundant). More efficient schemes include DSB-SC (carrier suppressed, efficiency 100% but bandwidth 2fm), SSB-SC (one sideband and carrier suppressed, bandwidth fm, efficiency 100% but requires sharp filter and coherent detection), VSB (vestigial sideband used in TV), and FM/digital schemes. Envelope detector for AM requires RC time constant satisfying 1/fc << RC << 1/fm to follow envelope while smoothing RF ripple; too large RC causes diagonal peak clipping, too small causes excessive RF ripple. Condition to avoid clipping: RC ≤ √(1-m²)/(m ωm).

Additional Analysis: Power Calculations and Efficiency Derivation

For AM wave vAM(t)=Vc[1+m cos(ωmt)]cos(ωct), average power into load R is:

Pt = <vAM²>/R = (Vc²/2R) * <[1+m cos(ωmt)]²> * <cos²(ωct)>? Actually average over both fast and slow variations gives Pt = Pc(1+m²/2), where Pc=Vc²/(2R) is carrier power. Derivation: vAM² = Vc²[1+2m cos(ωmt)+m² cos²(ωmt)]cos²(ωct). Averaging cos²(ωct)=1/2 and <cos(ωmt)>=0, <cos²(ωmt)>=1/2, so Pt = Vc²/(2R) * [1 + m²/2] = Pc(1+m²/2). Sideband power PSB = Pt - Pc = Pc m²/2, with each sideband Pc m²/4.

Efficiency η = PSB/Pt = (m²/2)/(1+m²/2) = m²/(2+m²). At m=0.25, η=0.0625/2.0625=3.03%, at m=0.5, η=0.25/2.25=11.11%, at m=0.75, η=0.5625/2.5625=21.95%, at m=1.0, η=1/3=33.33%, matching Table 303.2. Even at 100% modulation, 66.67% power wasted in carrier. Since average speech/music has m≈0.3-0.4, average efficiency <8%, explaining why AM broadcast transmitters require large power supplies and cooling for relatively small information power.

Over-Modulation and Splatter

When m>1, envelope attempts to go negative, causing carrier phase reversal. Mathematically, 1+m cos(ωmt) becomes negative during part of cycle, so vAM(t) = |1+m cos| * cos(ωct+π) (phase reversed). Simple diode envelope detector cannot detect phase reversal, as it only follows amplitude, so it produces clipped output with severe harmonic distortion. In frequency domain, over-modulation generates additional sidebands beyond fc±fm due to non-linear clipping, causing splatter into adjacent channels, which is prohibited by regulatory authorities. In broadcast, modulation is monitored and limited to m≤1 to avoid splatter and distortion. In this experiment, over-modulation at m=1.25 showed envelope crossover and phase inversion on oscilloscope, demonstrating why it must be avoided.

Triangle Wave Modulation

When modulating signal is triangle wave, its Fourier series contains odd harmonics: vtri(t) = (8Vm/π²)[cos(ωmt)/1² - cos(3ωmt)/3² + cos(5ωmt)/5² - ...]. AM with triangle therefore produces sidebands at fc±fm, fc±3fm, fc±5fm, etc., with amplitudes decreasing as 1/n². Envelope shape becomes diamond-shaped with straight-line segments, tracking linear ramp of triangle. This demonstrates that non-sinusoidal message expands occupied bandwidth beyond 2fm, requiring larger channel bandwidth. For arbitrary message with highest frequency fm_max, AM bandwidth is 2*fm_max, regardless of waveform shape, as long as message band-limited.

procedure: TPS-3421 trainer connected to regulated supply and power LEDs checked. Oscilloscope probe connected to carrier generator output on High position and carrier frequency adjusted to 800kHz sine wave of 4.0Vp-p with stable triggering.

DC multiplier linearity tested: variable DC Vi from 0.0V to 3.0V in 0.5V steps applied to modulation input, output carrier amplitude Vc measured and multiplier constant Ka = ΔVc/ΔVi computed. Ka found to be about 2.05 Vp-p/V, indicating linear operation of four-quadrant multiplier.

Audio signal generator output (1kHz sine) connected to AM modulator input. Oscilloscope CH1 connected to audio generator and CH2 to AM modulator output. Trigger source set to CH1 (modulating signal) to obtain stable envelope; triggering on RF caused jitter due to continuous amplitude variation.
Audio amplitude adjusted to achieve 50% modulation with Vmax=6.0Vp-p and Vmin=2.0Vp-p, giving m=(6-2)/(6+2)=0.50. Waveform recorded and sketched.

Modulation index varied systematically to target values m=0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00 and >1.00. For each, Vmax and Vmin measured with cursors, exact m calculated, and sideband power PSB, total power Pt and efficiency η% computed as in Table 303.2.

Over-modulation observed by increasing audio amplitude beyond m=1.0. Crossover points where upper and lower envelopes cross and carrier phase reversal of 180° during zero-crossing intervals noted, indicating distortion and splatter.
Modulating waveform switched from sine to symmetrical triangle wave. Diamond-shaped envelope with straight-line facets observed, tracking linear ramp of triangle wave, indicating harmonic sidebands.

Carrier selector switched to Low (30kHz) with modulating frequency 4kHz. Envelope with fewer RF cycles per audio period observed, making individual RF cycles distinguishable within envelope and illustrating carrier riding inside information boundary.
precautions: Oscilloscope trigger set to Channel 1 (audio modulating signal) rather than Channel 2 (RF AM signal) to avoid display jitter. Triggering on RF causes unstable envelope due to continuous amplitude variation.
Short ground clip leads used when probing 800kHz carrier to minimize parasitic inductance that causes ringing and incorrect Vmax readings.
Sum of DC offset and peak audio voltage kept below ±10V, the maximum input range of analog multiplier, to prevent internal clipping and non-linear distortion.
content.discussion:
Results obtained with TPS-3421 trainer agree with classical DSB-FC AM theory.

Multiplier linearity test (Table 303.1) showed constant sensitivity Ka≈2.05 Vp-p/V across 0-3V input, confirming envelope faithfully follows input audio without non-linear distortion. If Ka varied, intermodulation distortion would occur.

Table 303.2 and Graph 303.1 illustrate low efficiency of standard AM. At m=0.25, only 3.03% of total power carries information, 96.97% in carrier. Even at 100% modulation (m=1.0), efficiency only 33.33%. Average broadcast with m≈0.3-0.4 operates below 8% efficiency. This explains why modern systems use single-sideband suppressed carrier and FM for better power utilization.

Over-modulation (m=1.25) showed phase reversal when Vm>Vc. Term 1+mcos(ωmt) becomes negative during part of cycle, causing RF carrier to reverse phase by 180°. Diode envelope detector conducts only on positive half-cycles and cannot follow phase reversal, so recovered audio is clipped at zero baseline, generating harmonics that spill into adjacent channels as splatter and cause distortion.

When carrier switched to Low 30kHz with 4kHz modulating tone, fc/fm ratio dropped from 800:1 to 7.5:1. Each audio cycle contained fewer than 8 RF oscillations, making individual cycles visible within envelope. This highlights physical picture of carrier riding inside information boundary, less obvious at high fc where envelope appears smooth.

Practical observations: Triggering on audio rather than RF was essential for stable display. Long ground leads introduced ringing due to inductance resonating with probe capacitance, affecting Vmax measurement. Keeping ground lead short improved accuracy. Multiplier remained linear as long as input stayed within ±10V range.

The experiment demonstrates why AM broadcast requires large transmitter power but still has poor efficiency, and why over-modulation must be avoided to prevent adjacent-channel interference and audio distortion.

content.conclusion:
AM signals were successfully generated and analyzed across under-modulation, critical 100% modulation and over-modulation regimes. Modulation index formula m=(Vmax-Vmin)/(Vmax+Vmin) was verified using oscilloscope envelope measurements. Time-domain waveforms confirmed clean envelope for m<1, envelope touching zero for m=1 and phase reversal with clipping for m>1. Spectral analysis confirmed bandwidth BW=2fm, independent of carrier frequency. Power calculations verified maximum theoretical efficiency of DSB-FC is 33.33% at m=1.0, showing why suppressed-carrier schemes like SSB-SC and DSB-SC are preferred for power efficiency. Proper oscilloscope triggering and probing techniques for RF measurements were also practiced.

questions.question: Write the exact mathematical expressions for: (a) Carrier wave, (b) Modulating wave, and (c) Modulated AM wave.
questions.answer:
• Carrier: vc(t)=Vc cos(ωc t)=Vc cos(2π fc t) where Vc is unmodulated peak amplitude and fc is carrier frequency (800kHz in high position).
• Modulating: vm(t)=Vm cos(ωm t)=Vm cos(2π fm t) where Vm is peak modulating amplitude and fm is audio frequency (1kHz).
• Modulated AM: vAM(t)=[Vc+Vm cos(ωm t)]cos(ωc t)=Vc[1+m cos(ωm t)]cos(ωc t) where m=Vm/Vc. Expanded: vAM(t)=Vc cos(ωc t)+ (mVc/2)cos[2π(fc-fm)t] + (mVc/2)cos[2π(fc+fm)t] showing carrier plus two sidebands.

questions.question: What is the bandwidth of an AM signal? Prove it mathematically from the frequency spectrum.
questions.answer: From spectral expansion, AM consists of LSB at fc-fm, carrier at fc, USB at fc+fm. Bandwidth is highest minus lowest: BW = fUSB - fLSB = (fc+fm)-(fc-fm)=2fm. Hence bandwidth is twice modulating frequency, independent of carrier. For voice limited to 5kHz, AM channel bandwidth is 10kHz, which is why broadcast channels are spaced 9-10kHz.

questions.question: Compare the envelope of the modulated AM signal with the original audio generator signal. What happens when the modulating wave is switched to a triangle wave?
questions.answer: Upper envelope is Eupper(t)=Vc+Vm cos(ωm t). Subtracting DC offset Vc gives Vm cos(ωm t), replica of original audio in frequency, phase and shape, which is why envelope detector can recover audio. When switched to symmetrical triangle, envelope becomes diamond-shaped with straight-line facets, tracking linear dv/dt ramp of triangle. Spectrally, triangle contains odd harmonics fm,3fm,5fm with amplitudes decaying as 1/n², so AM spectrum produces harmonic sideband pairs at fc±fm, fc±3fm, fc±5fm, expanding occupied bandwidth.

questions.question: Explain the operation of an Envelope Diode Detector and derive the mathematical condition required to prevent "Diagonal Peak Clipping" distortion.
questions.answer: Envelope detector consists of half-wave diode in series with parallel RC low-pass (RL, CL). On positive RF peaks, diode forward biases and charges CL to peak. Between peaks, diode reverse biases and CL discharges through RL. For faithful demodulation, time constant τ=RLCL must satisfy RLCL >>1/fc to smooth RF ripple and RLCL <<1/fm to follow audio descending slope. If RLCL too large, capacitor discharges slower than envelope falling, diode remains reverse biased for several audio cycles and output follows exponential decay instead of audio - diagonal peak clipping. Condition: |dVC/dt|RC ≥ |dEenv/dt|max, giving RLCL ≤ √(1-m²)/(m ωm). For m=1, RC must be very small, so 100% modulation is critical.

learnings: Practical realization of frequency translation using analog multiplier to shift baseband audio to RF spectrum for wireless transmission.
Measurement of modulation index on oscilloscope using Vmax and Vmin cursor readings, standard technique in communications lab.
Importance of triggering on modulating signal rather than RF carrier for stable envelope display in RF measurements.
Quantitative understanding of power wastage in DSB-FC AM (max 33.33% efficiency) and motivation for single-sideband and FM architectures used in modern broadcasting.
